facts.title: The Newest Halogen Group
facts.text: Tennessine sits at the bottom of Group 17, the halogens, directly below astatine. Although it is classified as a halogen by its position in the periodic table, scientists predict its chemistry would be very different from chlorine or iodine because of extreme relativistic effects on its electrons. Some models suggest it might behave more like a semi-metal than a typical reactive nonmetal.

facts.title: Named After Tennessee
facts.text: Tennessine was named in honor of the U.S. state of Tennessee, recognizing the contributions of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Vanderbilt University, and the University of Tennessee to superheavy element research. The name was officially approved by IUPAC in November 2016. It is one of only two elements named after a U.S. state, the other being californium.

facts.title: A 2010 Russian-American Team
facts.text: Tennessine was first created in 2010 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia, through a collaboration with American laboratories. The team was led by Yuri Oganessian, after whom element 118, oganesson, is named. The discovery was officially confirmed by IUPAC and IUPAP in late 2015.

facts.title: Made From Rare Berkelium
facts.text: To create tennessine, scientists bombarded a target of berkelium-249 with a beam of calcium-48 ions. The berkelium itself was extraordinarily difficult to obtain, requiring about 250 days of production at Oak Ridge's High Flux Isotope Reactor plus months of purification. Only around 22 milligrams of this precious material were available, and it decays with a half-life of just 330 days.

facts.title: Vanishingly Few Atoms Ever Made
facts.text: Only a handful of tennessine atoms have ever existed since its discovery. Across multiple experiments, scientists have detected merely a few dozen atoms in total. Each one is identified not by seeing it directly, but by tracing the chain of alpha-particle decays it produces as it falls apart.

facts.title: Gone in Milliseconds
facts.text: Tennessine is intensely radioactive and extraordinarily short-lived. Its most stable known isotope, tennessine-294, has a half-life of only about 51 milliseconds, while tennessine-293 lasts around 22 milliseconds. Because it disappears almost instantly, no one has ever accumulated a weighable sample or directly studied its bulk properties.

facts.title: Sitting in the Eighth Row
facts.text: Tennessine is one of the elements completing the seventh period of the periodic table, alongside nihonium, moscovium, livermorium, and oganesson. With 117 protons, its electrons are predicted to fill orbitals up to the 7p shell. Filling the entire seventh row was a major milestone announced by IUPAC in 2016.

facts.title: A Probe of the Island of Stability
facts.text: Tennessine research is part of the search for the theorized island of stability, a region of superheavy elements predicted to have unusually long lifetimes. Adding neutrons toward the magic number of 184 is thought to boost stability, and tennessine isotopes help map the approach to that island. Studying its decay chains gives physicists clues about nuclear shell structure at the extreme edge of matter.

facts.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Electrons
facts.text: In superheavy atoms like tennessine, inner electrons move at a significant fraction of the speed of light, triggering Einstein's relativistic effects. These effects are predicted to split tennessine's outer 7p electrons into two energy groups, weakening its ability to form the classic minus-one ion typical of halogens. This is why chemists suspect tennessine would break the neat trends seen in fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine.

facts.title: Purely Synthetic and Practical-Use Free
facts.text: Tennessine does not occur anywhere in nature, not on Earth and not in stars, because any atoms formed would decay far too quickly to persist. It exists only when deliberately forged atom-by-atom in particle accelerators. It has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications, and its sole value is advancing fundamental science about the limits of the periodic table.
